We now know why puddles stop spreading.
For something that sounds so mundane, it's actually an interesting read. Thanks for sharing!

ELI5? I would have assumed it would have something to do with surface tension (and perhaps surface area?), but this line confused me "the liquid-solid and liquid-air interfaces start feeling each other."

I was thinking the same thing. Surface tension seems like the obvious answer, so why isn't that word even mentioned in the article? What is the difference between surface tension, and what the article describes?

I have a limited understanding, but did try to model bubble formation/nucleation in beer, once upon a time (when I was a physics student at a state university, and not the flagship campus... so not MIT). That said: this doesn't seem like it's anything new.

The article does not discuss "surface tension." It would seem surface tension is a false force emerging from solid-liquid, solid-gas, and liquid-gas surface interactions (energies). Consider water on glass in air (which we'll call 75% N2 and 25% O2). The water is polar and able to make up to 4 water-water bonds (via van der-waals force, iirc). In liquid (sorry for lack of citation on this, it's recollection from biochemistry, so please correct if wrong) water makes about 3.8 bonds, meaning it's quite coherent. The glass is also polar, but with a different separation of charges, so there it's some net attraction or repulsion energy at this interface. Finally the gas is non-polar (oil is also non-polar and forms little blobs in water, which minimizes the surface interaction between the two). So a non-polar gas has some repulsion energy at the interface with both the glass and the water. The interactions of all three of these material interfaces (plus gravity) determine the size (radius and height) of the puddle.

If only I knew that "we didn't know why puddles stop spreading," I'd be published right now.
